title: Why granite soil changes the taste of Central Victorian Shiraz
excerpt: Harcourt sits on a decomposed granite seam. It makes the vines work harder, the crops smaller and the Shiraz darker — here is what that actually does in the glass.
author: Tom Broughton
imageAlt: Vine rows on decomposed granite soil running toward the Harcourt hills at golden hour
body:
Harcourt sits on an old granite seam that runs up through the Mount Alexander Shire. When that granite breaks down it makes a coarse, pale, free-draining soil with very little to eat in it. Gardeners hate it. Vines, oddly enough, do their best work in it.

## Poor soil, small berries, more skin

A vine planted in rich soil grows leaves and water-filled fruit. A vine planted in decomposed granite has to send roots down a long way to find anything, and it gives up on making big berries. Smaller berries mean a higher ratio of skin to juice, and skin is where the colour, the tannin and most of the aroma live.

That is the whole trick. Nothing clever happens in our winery that isn't already decided in the paddock by February.

## What it tastes like

Central Victorian Shiraz grown on granite tends to land in a particular place: dark fruit rather than jammy fruit, a savoury edge that reads as pepper or dried herb, and tannins that are firm without being drying. It is medium to full bodied rather than enormous.

Compare it to Shiraz off deeper clay-loam soils in warmer parts of the state and the difference is mostly one of tension. Granite fruit keeps its acid. It stays lifted.

## Why it ripens slowly

Our oldest block sits at the lowest part of the property, which is also the coolest. Cold air pools there overnight. Those vines ripen a week or two behind everything else, and they yield less — which is why the Old Vine Shiraz only gets made in years when the fruit earns it, and why production caps out around 60 cases.

## How to taste it for yourself

Come on a Friday, Saturday or Sunday between 11am and 5pm. Ask for the Shiraz side by side with the Cabernet — same soil, same season, two different answers. Tastings are $10 and waived if you buy something.

title: What a vineyard wedding actually costs in Victoria
excerpt: Straight numbers, no packages you have to ring for. Here is what a wedding at a Central Victorian vineyard costs in 2026, what moves the price, and where couples usually overspend.
author: Sara Broughton
imageAlt: Wedding ceremony chairs set in an aisle between vine rows with granite hills behind
body:
Most vineyard venues make you fill in a form to find out the price. We think that wastes everybody's afternoon, so here are the figures.

## The short version

A ceremony and reception for 80 to 120 guests at Harcourt Valley runs between $8,900 and $12,400. A midweek or winter date starts around $6,500 for the same property and the same day-long access. A ceremony on its own, up to 40 guests, starts at $2,200.

## What moves the number

Three things, in order of how much they matter.

- Day of the week. A Saturday in autumn is the most expensive date we sell. A Friday in the same month can be a few thousand dollars less for an identical day.
- Season. March and April book first and cost most. July and August cost least, and the vines look better bare than people expect.
- Guest count. Not linearly — the jump from 80 to 120 costs less than people assume, because the venue hire is the same and only catering and glassware scale.

## What is included before you add anything

The whole property from 10am until midnight, and only one wedding a day. The ceremony site among the vines with 140 chairs set and packed away. The function room dressed for 120 seated or 180 standing. The old shearing shed as a genuine wet-weather plan. Long tables, cross-back chairs, linen and festoon lights. A coordinator on site from bump-in to the last dance. Parking for 60 cars.

## Where couples overspend

Flowers that get seen for two hours, and hire furniture the venue already owns. Ask any venue for their inventory list before you book a stylist — at our place the tables, chairs, linen and lighting are already in the hire, and a surprising number of couples pay twice for them.

## Where the money is worth it

Photography, and food. Nobody has ever told us they regretted feeding people properly.

## The next step is free

Come and stand where the ceremony would be. Bring your partner, taste the wine your guests would drink, and ask the awkward questions about wet weather and noise curfews in person. The tasting is on us, and we will hold a date for 14 days without a deposit while you think.

title: One day in the Bendigo wine region: a plan that actually works
excerpt: Thirty minutes from Bendigo, fifteen from Castlemaine, ninety from Melbourne. A realistic itinerary for a single day in Harcourt and the granite country around it.
author: Sara Broughton
imageAlt: Granite boulders and river red gums on the hillside above the Harcourt vineyard
body:
People routinely try to fit six cellar doors into a day and end up remembering none of them. Here is a plan that assumes you would rather enjoy three things than survive six.

## Getting here

Harcourt is on the Calder, roughly 90 minutes from Melbourne, 30 from Bendigo and 15 from Castlemaine. The Bendigo train stops at Castlemaine and Kyneton if you would rather not drive, and local taxis know the way to Schoolhouse Road.

## Morning: the granite

Start at the Harcourt granite quarries and the walking tracks on Mount Alexander. It takes an hour, it is free, and it explains everything you are about to taste. The soil in the vineyard is that same rock, broken down over a very long time.

## Late morning: cellar door

We open at 11am, Friday to Sunday. A tasting takes about 45 minutes at a sensible pace, costs $10 a head, and is waived if you take something home. Ask to taste the Shiraz against the Cabernet — they grew 200 metres apart.

## Lunch

Bring something, or pick up lunch in Castlemaine on the way through. There are tables in the garden and we will happily open something cold to go with whatever you have brought.

## Afternoon: apples, then Castlemaine

Harcourt is apple country as much as wine country, and the roadside orchards are worth the stop in season. Castlemaine's galleries and the botanical gardens will fill the rest of the afternoon comfortably.

## Practical notes

Cellar door is open Friday to Sunday, 11am to 5pm. The tasting room is wheelchair accessible and there is parking on site. Ring ahead on (03) 5474 2210 if you are bringing a group of more than eight.

title: How to plan a long-table dinner that doesn't feel like a function
excerpt: One table, forty to eighty people, and no lectern. What we have learned from hosting long-table dinners in a shearing shed, and the details that decide whether it works.
author: Tom Broughton
imageAlt: A single long banquet table dressed with linen and festoon lights inside the function shed
body:
A long-table dinner is not a gala with fewer tables. It is a different shape of evening, and the things that make it work are mostly unglamorous.

## One table, or it isn't one

The moment you split into two tables you have made a function. Keep everybody on a single run, even if it means a room that looks too narrow on the floor plan. Forty to eighty people is the sweet spot — beyond that the ends stop being part of the same night.

## Sit people down early

Long tables die when guests stand around for 90 minutes first. Half an hour of drinks, then sit. The conversation starts faster and the food arrives while people are still hungry.

## Serve it in the middle

Shared platters down the centre beat plated courses for this format, every time. People pass things, which means they talk to the person next to them without being told to.

## Keep the speeches short and early

Between the first and second course, standing where everyone can see you, no microphone if the room allows it. Two minutes each. If somebody needs ten minutes, that is a different event.

## The practical bits at our place

We seat 40 to 80 on one table in the old shearing shed, five courses with matched pours from around $120 a head. Trestles, linen, cross-back chairs, festoon lights and the sound system are in the hire. You get the property from 10am to midnight, and bump-in the day before if you need it. Catering can be ours or yours — both genuinely work.

## The thing people forget

Heating in winter and shade in February. Ask any venue about both before you sign, because a beautiful room at the wrong temperature is the only detail your guests will remember.

title: Cellar door etiquette at a small family winery
excerpt: You are not expected to know anything. A plain guide to tasting at a small winery — what to ask, whether you have to buy, spitting, kids, dogs and the rest.
author: Sara Broughton
imageAlt: Red wine being poured into a glass at the timber cellar door bar
body:
The most common thing we hear at the bar is some version of "sorry, I don't really know much about wine." Nobody needs to apologise for that. Here is everything you actually need to know.

## Do you have to buy something?

No. A tasting is $10 a head and we waive it if you buy a bottle, which is the whole of the pressure. Plenty of people taste, say thanks and leave, and they are welcome back.

## What should I ask?

"What should I try if I usually drink X" is the single best question at any cellar door. It tells the person pouring where to start and saves you working through six wines that were never going to suit you.

## Am I allowed to spit?

Yes, and if you are driving you should. There is a bucket on the bar for exactly that reason and using it is a sign you know what you are doing, not the opposite.

## How long does it take?

About 45 minutes for the full range at an unhurried pace. Come before 4pm if you want time to talk.

## Kids, dogs, groups

Kids are fine and there is grass to run on. Dogs on leads are fine outside. Groups of more than eight, ring ahead on (03) 5474 2210 so we can have someone free for you.

## Can I take wine away that I can't buy anywhere else?

Usually, yes. The Old Vine Shiraz is capped at 60 cases and the Rosé sells out most years before the next vintage is ready — cellar door is generally the only place either of them exists.

## When are you open?

Friday, Saturday and Sunday, 11am to 5pm, at 41 Schoolhouse Rd, Harcourt. Functions and weddings run by arrangement on other days.

title: Vintage 2026: a report from the oldest vines in the shire
excerpt: A cool, slow, late season on the granite. What the 2026 harvest looked like across the blocks, what we picked and when, and which wines it is likely to become.
author: Tom Broughton
imageAlt: French oak barrels resting in the cool granite cellar at Harcourt Valley
body:
Vintage 2026 was late, cool and slower than we are used to, which on granite is usually good news.

## The season

A wet spring meant we spent more time in the rows than in the shed through October and November. Flowering ran a week behind. Summer never really got angry — we had four days over 35 degrees where we would normally expect a dozen, and cool nights right through February.

That combination does two things: it holds acid, and it lets flavour catch up with sugar instead of racing ahead of it.

## Picking dates

Riesling came in first, in the second week of March, cold and early in the morning as always. Chardonnay followed about ten days later. The Shiraz blocks ran from late March into the first week of April, and the old block at the bottom of the property — as usual, the last thing standing — came in on 9 April.

## The old vines

The 1975 plantings are the oldest in the Mount Alexander Shire and they sit at the lowest, coolest part of the property. They yield very little and ripen last. In 2026 they gave us small, thick-skinned fruit with good natural acid, which is exactly the profile that justifies making an Old Vine Shiraz at all.

We will make the call after the wine has been in French oak for a while, but early signs are good. Production, as always, would cap at 60 cases.

## What to expect in bottle

Whites with more line and less weight than 2025. Rosé that should be bright and dry. Reds that look darker and more structured than the season felt — small berries again — and that will want a year or two more than usual before they show their best.

## When you can taste it

The whites will be at cellar door before summer. The reds will take their time, and so will we.
